lmsArticle.title: The 8 Fallacies of Distributed Systems
lmsArticle.subtitle: The Network is Reliable. Latency is Zero. Bandwidth is Infinite. If you believe these, your system will fail. We debunk the 8 fallacies.
lmsArticle.excerpt:
TLDR

TLDR: In 1994, L. Peter Deutsch at Sun Microsystems listed 8 assumptions that developers make about distributed systems — all of which are false. Believing them leads to hard-to-reproduce bugs,
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

The first time I heard "the network is reliable", I nodded. The second time was when our payment service was retrying duplicate charges because the network wasn't reliable and we hadn't handled it. Orders were double-billed, customers called support, and the root cause traced back to a single missing idempotency check — a check that would have been obvious if we had taken this fallacy seriously from day one. These 8…

This walkthrough focuses on **The Eight Assumptions That Will Break Your System**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- The first time I heard "the network is reliable", I nodded.
- The second time was when our payment service was retrying duplicate charges because the network wasn't reliable and we hadn't handled it.
- Orders were double-billed, customers called support, and the root cause traced back to a single missing idempotency check — a check that would have been obvious if we had taken this fallacy seriously from day one.

**Concepts in play:** consistency-replication, circuit-breaker, system-design-hld-architectures, caching

## Stage 1 — What Makes a System "Distributed" in the First Place

- Before the fallacies can bite you, you need to know what kind of system exposes you to them.
- A distributed system is any application where components run on separate machines and communicate over a network.
- That sounds obvious — until you realise it covers microservices, mobile apps talking to a backend, two data centre regions sharing a database, and even a monolith that makes third-party API calls.
- The key insight: a network call is fundamentally different from a function call.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The key insight: a network call is fundamentally different from a function call.

## Stage 2 — Network Fallacies 1–4: Reliability, Latency, Bandwidth, and Security

- Fallacy 1: The network is reliable.
- A single function call that succeeds 99.9% of the time fails once every 1,000 requests, and distributed systems call each other thousands of times per second.
- Design response: Retry with exponential backoff.
- Use circuit breakers (Hystrix, Resilience4j).

*Applies **circuit-breaker** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Use circuit breakers (Hystrix, Resilience4j).

## Stage 3 — Infrastructure Fallacies 5–8: Topology, Administration, Cost, and Compatibility

- Fallacy 5: Topology doesn't change.
- Auto-scaling adds and removes instances.
- Hardcoding IP addresses breaks as soon as a node is replaced.
- Design response: Use service discovery (Consul, Kubernetes DNS, AWS Cloud Map).

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Design response: Use service discovery (Consul, Kubernetes DNS, AWS Cloud Map).

## Stage 4 — From False Assumption to Production Outage

- Every fallacy follows the same lifecycle: the assumption goes unchallenged in local development, test environments mask the problem, and then production traffic amplifies the gap until something fails.
- The painful part: teams almost always reach R — but only after the outage forces their hand.
- The goal of knowing these fallacies is to reach R before the first incident, not after.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F[False Assumption baked into code] --> D[No defensive code written]
    D --> T[Tests pass on localhost / staging]
    T --> P[Hits real production traffic]
    P --> O[Outage or silent data corruption]
    O --> M[Team adds retry / circuit breaker / mTLS]
    M --> R[Resilient system]
```

**Observable outcome:** The goal of knowing these fallacies is to reach R before the first incident, not after.

## Stage 5 — Real-World Applications: Where Each Fallacy Bites in Production

- Abstract warnings become concrete when mapped to documented production failures.
- A new service failing in all eight ways simultaneously is rare.
- A new service failing in two or three of them in the first quarter after launch is extremely common.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** A new service failing in two or three of them in the first quarter after launch is extremely common.

## Stage 6 — A Pre-Flight Checklist for Every New Service Call

- Use this at design-review time to catch fallacy violations before they reach production.
- Reliability and latency (Fallacies 1 & 2) - [ ] Timeout configured explicitly (never rely on OS defaults) - [ ] Retry with exponential backoff and random jitter - [ ] Circuit breaker so a failing downstream cannot exhau…

*Applies **circuit-breaker** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Reliability and latency (Fallacies 1 & 2) - [ ] Timeout configured explicitly (never rely on OS defaults) - [ ] Retry with exponential backoff and random jitter - [ ] Circuit breaker so a failing downstream cannot exhau…

## End-to-end outcome

The first time I heard "the network is reliable", I nodded.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Choosing Your Defenses Against the 8 Fallacies

Map each fallacy to a specific architectural defense.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Deep Dive: The Practical Antidote for Distributed Failures

- **Detection:** The minimal production checklist for every service call: - Timeout set (never rely on OS default) - Retry with exponential backoff + jitter - Circuit breaker to stop cascade - Bulkhead (limit concurr…
- **User or operator impact:** The minimal production checklist for every service call: - Timeout set (never rely on OS default) - Retry with exponential backoff + jitter - Circuit breaker to stop cascade - Bulkhead (limit concurr…

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Why These Fallacies Persist

- **Detection:** These fallacies are taught in university — and still violated in code every week because: - Local development masks network problems (everything runs on localhost) - Unit tests don't simulate network…
- **User or operator impact:** These fallacies are taught in university — and still violated in code every week because: - Local development masks network problems (everything runs on localhost) - Unit tests don't simulate network…

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
